metadata.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
metadata.document_title: Clinical Guidance on Asthma: Pathophysiology, Reliever vs Controller Inhaler Therapy, and Acute Exacerbation Protocols

sections.text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the conducting airways characterized by recurrent episodes of bronchial hyperresponsiveness, reversible airflow obstruction, and chronic airway inflammation. Clinical symptoms include episodic expiratory wheezing, dyspnea (shortness of breath), chest tightness, and a dry or productive cough that is characteristically worse at night or early in the morning. Symptoms are triggered by viral upper respiratory infections, inhaled environmental allergens (dust mites, pollen, animal dander), cold air, physical exercise, tobacco smoke, and occupational irritants. Confirmation of diagnosis relies on demonstrating reversible airflow limitation on spirometry (FEV1 increase >= 12% and >= 200 mL following bronchodilator inhalation).

sections.section_title: Stepwise Pharmacotherapy: Controller vs Reliever Medications
sections.text: Asthma management requires distinguishing daily maintenance controllers from rapid-acting as-needed relievers: 1. Controller Medications (Anti-inflammatory Maintenance): Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS e.g., Fluticasone, Budesonide, Beclomethasone) represent the cornerstone of chronic therapy. Regular daily use suppresses airway mucosal inflammation, reduces exacerbations, and prevents airway remodeling. ICS is commonly combined with a Long-Acting Beta-2 Agonist (LABA e.g., Formoterol, Salmeterol) in moderate-to-severe persistent asthma; 2. Reliever Medications (Acute Bronchodilation): Short-Acting Beta-2 Agonists (SABA e.g., Salbutamol / Albuterol 100-200 mcg via pressurized metered-dose inhaler with a spacer) provide rapid relaxation of airway smooth muscle during acute bronchospasm. Alternatively, low-dose ICS-formoterol is utilized as both maintenance and reliever therapy (SMART protocol).

sections.section_title: Acute Asthma Exacerbation and Life-Threatening Red Flags
sections.text: An acute asthma attack represents a severe clinical deterioration requiring urgent stepped intervention. Management includes high-dose inhaled SABA (4 to 10 puffs of Salbutamol via spacer every 20 minutes for 1 hour), systemic corticosteroids (oral Prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days) to resolve mucosal edema, and supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 93-95%. Critical life-threatening red flags indicating impending respiratory arrest and requiring immediate emergency intensive care transfer include: 1. Inability to speak in full sentences or breathlessness at rest; 2. Respiratory rate > 25 breaths per minute; 3. Tachycardia > 110 beats per minute; 4. Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) < 50% of predicted or personal best; 5. 'Silent Chest' (absence of wheezing due to severe airflow limitation and respiratory muscle exhaustion), cyanosis, confusion, or drowsiness.
